profile.name: Sivas bar
profile.tagline: Courtly and sacred artistic traditions of the 18th-century Ahom monarchy in Assam.
profile.insight: In 1722, Ahom King Siva Singha transferred royal governance to Queen Phuleswari, a dancer of the Nat caste who assumed the title of Bar Raja.
profile.profile: The artistic and ceremonial traditions associated with the reign of King Siva Singha (1714–1744) reflect a significant era of music and dance patronage in 18th-century Assam. Under royal decrees and the leadership of Queen Phuleswari—who hailed from the Nat caste of dancers—court arts and Sakta religious rituals were integrated into royal life. Foreign musicians were invited to instruct court performers, while the monarch himself authored pious songs. Specific choreographic steps for Sivas bar remain unrecorded in historical source texts, leaving physical movement details undescribed.
profile.profile_long:
The period of King Siva Singha (1714–1744), also known as Sutanpha, marks a transformative epoch in the cultural history of the Ahom kingdom in Assam. Ascending the throne following the death of his father Rudra Singha, Siva Singha oversaw a peaceful reign distinguished by intense religious devotion, architectural construction, and extensive patronage of literature, music, and performance arts. A defining moment occurred in 1722 when astrologers predicted the end of his rule due to chatra-bhanga-yoga. To evade this omen, Siva Singha installed his chief queen, Phuleswari, with supreme authority under the title of Bar Raja. Phuleswari, who belonged to the traditional Nat caste of dancers, brought performing arts background directly to the center of royal governance. Her elevation marked a unique historic intersection between traditional dancer communities and sovereign political power.

Specific choreography, step patterns, and movement formations for Sivas bar are not described in sources. Historical records focus primarily on the political, religious, and musical ecosystem within which performance arts functioned rather than step-by-step physical manuals. Performance traditions of this era were intimately linked to court ceremonies and temple rituals, particularly those of Sakta Hinduism supported by the royal court and Brahmin priests such as Krishnaram Bhattacharjya (Parbatiya Gosain).

Music held a prominent place during Siva Singha's reign. The monarch invited foreign musicians into the Ahom kingdom to instruct native musicians and refine court musical traditions. Siva Singha himself was a composer, authoring a substantial collection of pious songs dedicated to religious worship. Royal patronage also fostered monumental literary and artistic works, including the illustrated manuscript Hastividyarnava. Instrumentation and musical structures accompanying performance traditions were embedded within courtly and temple devotional practices, though technical musical transcriptions are not detailed in the available records.

Performers during this era operated within both royal palaces and sacred temple complexes. Key settings included the capital Rangpur, the Kamakhya Temple atop Nilachal hill, and regional sites such as the Balilecha Kali Mandir in Ballilesha village. Attire for court and ritual dancers reflected the social and religious status of 18th-century Ahom court culture, though precise costume specifications for Sivas bar are not described in sources.

Occasions for music and performance centered around state rituals, royal assemblies, and major religious celebrations such as Durga Puja. Queen Phuleswari's zealous promotion of Saktism led to organized rituals at the capital, where court and religious figures were assembled for ceremonial observances. These events served both spiritual objectives and political expressions of royal power across the kingdom.

Key figures of this period include King Siva Singha, Queen Phuleswari (Pramatheswari), and subsequent queens who held the title of Bar Raja, including Ambika and Sarbeswari. The religious guidance of Parbatiya Gosain shaped the court's ceremonial choices, while traditional artists of the Nat caste provided the foundational performing arts talent of the era.

Regional variations in performance traditions corresponded to regional administrative and temple centers established under Ahom land grants. While performance was concentrated in Rangpur and major Sakti Peeth sites, local variations across Assam are not described in sources.

Lineage and inheritance of these cultural traditions stem from the broader Ahom dynastic heritage and the traditional hereditary status of the Nat dancer caste. While later political upheavals—such as the Moamoria rebellion—altered the kingdom's social landscape, the patronage model established under Siva Singha left a lasting legacy on Assamese sacred architecture, music, and manuscript arts.

sections.origins_and_history: King Siva Singha (Sutanpha) ruled the Ahom kingdom from 1714 to 1744. In 1722, advised by astrologers regarding an adverse cosmic alignment (chatra-bhanga-yoga), he passed sovereign authority to his chief queen Phuleswari, who belonged to the Nat caste of traditional dancers. She took the name Pramatheswari and the title Bar Raja, marking a major historical instance of a dancer holding supreme royal power. Subsequent queens Ambika and Sarbeswari also served as Bar Raja.

Musical patronage flourished alongside manuscript production such as the Hastividyarnava. Specific instrument names and rhythmic meters are not described in sources.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performances occurred in royal court settings such as Rangpur and sacred sites including Kamakhya Temple and Balilecha Kali Mandir. Specific costume materials, garments, and adornments are not described in sources.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Dance and music during this reign were closely tied to Sakta religious rituals, Durga Puja observances, and royal court ceremonies. Performance served both state political functions and religious devotion.
sections.notable_figures: Notable figures include King Siva Singha (Sutanphaa), Queen Phuleswari (Bar Raja / Pramatheswari, from the Nat dancer caste), Queen Ambika, Queen Sarbeswari, and the Shakta priest Krishnaram Bhattacharjya (Parbatiya Gosain).

episode_brief.title_hook: The Dancer Who Ruled an Empire
episode_brief.logline: Explore how 18th-century Ahom King Siva Singha elevated a court dancer of the Nat caste to supreme ruler, shaping devotional music and royal ritual in Assam.
beats: Introduction to the Ahom kingdom in 1714 and the accession of King Siva Singha.
The astrological prophecy of 1722 and the appointment of Queen Phuleswari as Bar Raja.
Examination of Queen Phuleswari's origins in the Nat caste of traditional dancers.
The royal invitation to foreign musicians and King Siva Singha's composition of pious songs.
Visits to historical Sakta sites established during the reign, such as Balilecha Kali Mandir.

18th-century Ahom temple architecture and copper plate inscriptions
Historical coinage minted under Queen Phuleswari and King Siva Singha

claims.text: Siva Singha ruled as Ahom King from 1714 until his death on December 14, 1744.
claims.quote: Siva Singha (died 14 December 1744), also known as Sutanpha, was Ahom King from 1714 until his death in 1744.

claims.text: King Siva Singha endowed Queen Phuleshwari, who belonged to the Nat caste of dancers, with the title of Bar Raja.
claims.quote: consented to endow his chief queen Phuleshwari, a Nat by caste (a caste of dancers), with the supreme vest, who assumed the name Pramatheswari and the title of Bar Raja.

claims.text: Foreign musicians were brought to court to provide instruction, and King Siva Singha authored a collection of pious songs.
claims.quote: Foreign musicians were invited into his country to instruct his own and the Monarch became the author of a large collection of pious songs.
